replying_to: Replying to Accuracy-First Rényi Differential Privacy and Post-Processing Immunity
display_title: Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer 3cjJ

summary.value: The paper formally proves the PPI guarantee of some existing accuracy-first RDP/DP notions and introduces a new notion, ex-post RDP, which involves the $\epsilon$ as part of the output. The new privacy notion satisfies PPI.

strengths.value:
The paper identifies a concrete invariance gap in ex-post privacy guarantees and proposes a clean, easy notion by treating the realized bound as part of the output and formalize PPI. The ex-post RDP's framework is tidy, creative recombination that satisfies PPI.

They formally proves the PPI property of some important existing accuracy-first privacy notions.

weaknesses.value:
# W1:

While the paper is framed as "accuracy-first", the concrete contribution is primarily a definitional/packaging fix (carrying the per-run certificate and proving PPI on (Y,$\epsilon$)). The work does not yet advance accuracy per se (no new calibration/mechanism or demonstrated utility gains at fixed privacy). In addition, the experiments are limited and do not support the "accuracy-first" narrative.


In Related Work, the ordermeter literature is merely conceptually adjacent, but the present paper's technical contributions do not build on odometers. So, the discussion here is mostly contextual but feels disconnected from the paper's position. 



# W2:

My main concern is as follow.


The paper pointing out a limitation of existing ex-post notations: after post-processing, we often cannot construct a non-vacuous $E'(Y')$ (see the example of Brownian mechanism's "$T$" issue in Page 5 of the paper). 


However, it seems that the root cause is the lack of bookkeeping the privacy parameter/certificate, rather than an intrinsic or fundamental limiation of the existing notions (except the $\delta$-approximate ex-post).

The proposed fix is to treat the realized bound as part of the output and requireing it to be copied through post-processing. This is best viewed as an interface/notation repair, not a new privacy notion with new privatization mechanism nor an impossibility result. 


In practice, the post-processing functions/algorithms operates independently of $\epsilon$. The only requirement is to carry the certificate tag $\epsilon$ with the output so that an auditor at the end of the pipeline can attest the same per-run guarantee.


While the theory is clear (though not, in my view, especially significant), the experiments are narrow illustrations (Adult synthetic data) and do not substantiate the paper’s "accuracy-first" framing or demonstrate utility gains at fixed privacy against strong baselines. Thus, the experiments do not support the broader claims.


Overall, the contribution feels illustrative rather than substantive: a neat packaging/notation fix with a small-scale demo, but not yet a result that moves practice or theory.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer 3cjJ

comment.value:
Thank you for the review.

> While the paper is framed as "accuracy-first", the concrete contribution is primarily a definitional/packaging fix (carrying the per-run certificate and proving PPI on (Y, $\epsilon$)). The work does not yet advance accuracy per se (no new calibration/mechanism or demonstrated utility gains at fixed privacy). In addition, the experiments are limited and do not support the "accuracy-first" narrative.

We make several advancements to the accuracy-first perspective:
- We prove post-processing immunity for any ex-post privacy definition for the first time and show the shortcomings of several existing ex-post privacy definitions.
- We give the first proof that the Brownian mechanism satisfies an ex-post definition with post-processing immunity, enabling accuracy-first DP with practical noise-reduction techniques.
- We propose the first mechanism that allows checking accuracy on a private validation dataset that is disjoint from the training dataset. The previous mechanism from Ligett et al. (2017) and Whitehouse et al. (2022) can only check training accuracy, not validation accuracy.
- The experiments support the accuracy-first perspective by demonstrating the above with a practical example.

> In Related Work, the ordermeter literature is merely conceptually adjacent, but the present paper's technical contributions do not build on odometers. So, the discussion here is mostly contextual but feels disconnected from the paper's position.

It is true that we do not build on odometers, but we believe discussing this connection, as in Appendix A, is still helpful for readers and clarifies the relationship between ex-post privacy and odometers.

> The paper pointing out a limitation of existing ex-post notations: after post-processing, we often cannot construct a non-vacuous $E’(Y’)$ (see the example of Brownian mechanism's "$T$" issue in Page 5 of the paper).

> However, it seems that the root cause is the lack of bookkeeping the privacy parameter/certificate, rather than an intrinsic or fundamental limiation of the existing notions (except the $\delta$-approximate ex-post).
The proposed fix is to treat the realized bound as part of the output and requireing it to be copied through post-processing. This is best viewed as an interface/notation repair, not a new privacy notion with new privatization mechanism nor an impossibility result.

> In practice, the post-processing functions/algorithms operates independently of $\epsilon$. The only requirement is to carry the certificate tag $\epsilon$ with the output so that an auditor at the end of the pipeline can attest the same per-run guarantee.

We agree that our new notation is repairing the interface the previous works used. This is why we present Definition 3.1 as a version of Definition 2.4, not as a completely new privacy notion.

However, the new notation is not the main contribution of our paper, it is only one fix that the rest of our theory needs. Our main contributions are investigating the post-processing immunity of the existing ex-post privacy definitions, and developing theory for ex-post RDP that allows developing practical mechanisms.

> While the theory is clear (though not, in my view, especially significant), the experiments are narrow illustrations (Adult synthetic data) and do not substantiate the paper’s "accuracy-first" framing or demonstrate utility gains at fixed privacy against strong baselines. Thus, the experiments do not support the broader claims.

We are planning to add an extra experiment showing that our theory enables implementing an ex-post variant of DP-SGD. 

In general, using a fixed ex-ante privacy bound would not make sense, since the point of ex-post privacy is that the privacy bound is flexible. We are also the first to generate synthetic data under any ex-post privacy definition to our knowledge, so we are not aware of any appropriate baseline for ex-post synthetic data generation.

> Overall, the contribution feels illustrative rather than substantive: a neat packaging/notation fix with a small-scale demo, but not yet a result that moves practice or theory.

Our main contribution is neither the notation fix or the experiment, but the investigation of post-processing immunity and the other theory that makes the experiment possible. We believe they move both practice and theory. In particular, proving post-processing immunity for some ex-post privacy definitions fixes a major theoretical gap for them, and allows practitioners to use these definitions without needing to assume post-processing immunity.

display_title: Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer f84H

summary.value: This paper advocates a practical shift in how differential privacy is used in ML training: instead of fixing a privacy budget and measuring performance afterward, it proposes an accuracy-first paradigm where the training process dynamically adjusts the privacy parameters until a target accuracy is achieved, then computes the final privacy level using Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP).

strengths.value:
1. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets show improved accuracy while maintaining reasonable privacy levels.
2. The authors’ accuracy-first framing is intuitive and addresses a real deployment gap between theoretical guarantees and practitioner needs.

weaknesses.value: There seems to be a lack of variance or sensitivity analysis (e.g., different α values in RDP) to confirm the stability of the bounds (robustness).

questions.value: It would be better to clarify the variance or sensitivity analysis (e.g., different α values in RDP) to confirm the stability of the bounds (robustness).

comment.value:
Thank you for the review.

> There seems to be a lack of variance or sensitivity analysis (e.g., different α values in RDP) to confirm the stability of the bounds (robustness).

> It would be better to clarify the variance or sensitivity analysis (e.g., different α values in RDP) to confirm the stability of the bounds (robustness).

For the plain Gaussian accuracy check + Brownian mechanism, the total $\epsilon$ is a linear function of $\alpha$. For the SVT accuracy check + Brownian mechanism, the total $\epsilon$ is an affine function of $\alpha$. We have added the precise functions to the end of Appendix D. These can be expressed in an ex-post variant of zCDP, which satisfies similar properties as ex-post RDP. We have also added this discussion to Appendix D.

display_title: Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer coYK

summary.value: This paper addresses post-processing immunity (PPI) within the ``accuracy-first'' paradigm of DP. It first shows that existing practical ex-post privacy definitions do not satisfy PPI. To resolve this, the authors introduce a new notation that treats the privacy bound $\epsilon$ as part of the algorithm's output. Using this notation, they propose a new definition, ex-post Rényi DP, and show that it satisfies PPI. The paper also provides a new privacy analysis for the existing Brownian mechanism, showing that it satisfies ex-post RD by proving its equivalence to a simpler sequential mechanism.

strengths.value:
- The extension to ex-post RDP is natural.
- I believe the results are sound (at least by intuition), though I did not check every detail in the Appendices.
- Both theoretical and experimental results are provided.

weaknesses.value:
- The paper does not propose any novel algorithm specially designed for the new ex-post RDP framework, focusing instead on re-analyzing an existing one.
- The empirical evaluation lacks a comparative analysis against other established privacy notions, so it is unclear if the framework offers a superior privacy-utility tradeoff in practice.
- The paper lacks discussion on the limitations of the ex-post RDP notion.

questions.value:
- From a theoretical perspective, does the ex-post RDP notion provide a better or worse privacy-utility tradeoff, while comparing with other accuracy-first notions? What is the cost of PPI here?
- The privacy guarantee is now a random variable. How should practitioners interpret, report, or compare such guarantees? For example, if we have two mechanisms, each with a different distribution of $\epsilon$, how do we decide which one is ``more private''?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer coYK

comment.value:
Thank you for the review.

> The paper does not propose any novel algorithm specially designed for the new ex-post RDP framework, focusing instead on re-analyzing an existing one.

We are the first to propose an algorithm to check an accuracy threshold under ex-post privacy on a validation set that is separate from the training set (Theorem 4.6 and Appendix D). While this is a combination of existing mechanisms, we view the possibility of combining existing mechanisms with our theory a strength rather than a weakness. After all, it is much easier to pick suitable well-known mechanisms and combine them using our theory than it is to design a mechanism specifically for ex-post RDP.

> The empirical evaluation lacks a comparative analysis against other established privacy notions, so it is unclear if the framework offers a superior privacy-utility tradeoff in practice.

> From a theoretical perspective, does the ex-post RDP notion provide a better or worse privacy-utility tradeoff, while comparing with other accuracy-first notions? What is the cost of PPI here?

We have added a comparison of our RDP-based bound for the Brownian mechanism with the bounds of Whitehouse et al. (2022) to Section 5. To make the comparison with a common yardstick, we convert all bounds to approximate ex-post privacy. Note that this conversion for probabilistic ex-post privacy has not been proven rigorously, but the conversion holds for the ex-ante versions of those definitions, and we conjecture it also holds in the same way for the ex-post definitions.

The results in Figure 1 show that all of the bounds are very similar when all free parameters in each bound are optimised separately for each noise variance. This means that there is no cost of post-processing immunity or the extra flexibility our RDP-based theory provides.

Besides, as we argue in the Introduction and the beginning of Section 3, and as several other authors argue (Mironov 2017, Meiser 2018, Dong et al. 2022), any sensible privacy definition should have post-processing immunity. As a result, it should be viewed as a requirement of privacy, not  something you would trade off for better utility.

> The paper lacks discussion on the limitations of the ex-post RDP notion.

Ex-post RDP shares the limitations of ex-ante RDP. First, RDP is hard to interpret. While we have an interpretation of ex-post RDP that is similar to the ex-ante interpretation of Mironov (2017) in Appendix B, it is not as clear as $f$-DP for example. However, an ex-post version of $f$-DP, or a special case like Gaussian DP (GDP), does not currently exist. This is one of the reasons we think developing ex-post  GDP or $f$-DP is a promising direction for future work.

A second limitation of RDP over approximate DP or $f$-DP is that converting RDP to those definitions is lossy in the ex-ante case. We conjecture this also holds in the ex-post case. However, currently the only way to obtain an approximate ex-post privacy guarantee for the Brownian mechanism is converting our RDP guarantee, but future work may be able to improve this if it is possible to analyse the Brownian mechanism in approximate ex-post privacy directly, or in an ex-post version of GDP.

We have added a paragraph discussing these to Section 7.

> The privacy guarantee is now a random variable. How should practitioners interpret, report, or compare such guarantees? For example, if we have two mechanisms, each with a different distribution of $\epsilon$, how do we decide which one is ``more private''?

This is a very good question that is equally relevant for all ex-post privacy notions. In practice, an ex-post mechanism returns some number $\epsilon$, which should be reported, along with the definition the mechanism satisfies and ideally details of how the $\epsilon$ was computed. For ex-post RDP, we give an interpretation of $\epsilon$ and $\alpha$ in Appendix B.

When comparing runs of ex-post mechanisms, one can just compare the returned $\epsilon$ values and say that the smaller $\epsilon$ is more private. The more difficult case is comparing mechanisms, as the $\epsilon$ is then a random variable as you wrote. A major difficulty is the fact that the distribution of $\epsilon$ depends on the private data, so to even have concrete distributions to compare, a prior over the data is needed (comparing $\epsilon$ distributions with the private data could leak privacy). If such a prior can be established, it then possible to compare for example the means of $\epsilon$ distributions, or their CDFs.

Since this question is equally relevant for all ex-post privacy definitions and does not have an easy answer, we believe it is best left for future work. We have added discussion of this to Section 7.

display_title: Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer GHWG

summary.value: This paper investigates post-processing immunity (PPI) under accuracy-first ex-post DP.  In contrast to conventional DP, ex-post DP allows different privacy loss on different outputs through a function $\mathcal{E}:Y\to \mathbb{R}$, and post-processing would change the output space and lose meaningful privacy loss, e.g., multiple $y$ collapse to one.  This paper proposes post-processing that outputs not only the function of $Y$ but also the privacy loss $\epsilon$, which addresses the output collapse issue.  Under this new notion, they prove that the pure ex-post DP and Rényi DP satisfy PPI, but the $\delta$- probabilistic ex-post DP does not.  For Renyi DP, they also prove adaptive composition and analyze the Brownian mechanism.

strengths.value:
- Making $\epsilon$ part of the output and defining post-processing is a nice way to handle post-processing.  
- Though scattered around the literature, the paper gives a clean survey on PPI on various ex-post DP.

weaknesses.value:
- The motivation of outputting $\epsilon$ is limited.  It seems like theory-first and departs from the conventional usage of post-process.  In practice, do people post-process data but also output all privacy loss in the previous post-process and composition $\epsilon_{1:K}$ as Theorem 4.5?  
- The exploration of the composition theorem is partial.  There is no composition theorem for pure ex‑post privacy analogous to Theorems 4.4–4.6.

questions.value: Can you prove adaptive composition for pure and approximate ex‑post DP, or provide counterexamples/conditions?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission4406 by Reviewer GHWG

comment.value:
Thank you for the review.

> The motivation of outputting $\epsilon$ is limited. It seems like theory-first and departs from the conventional usage of post-process. In practice, do people post-process data but also output all privacy loss in the previous post-process and composition $\epsilon_{1:K}$ as Theorem 4.5?

Releasing the intermediate $\epsilon_{1:K}$ values is not required in Theorem 4.5. Whether they should be released depends on the application. For example, if one just releases the final synthetic dataset, as in our experiment, there may not be a practical need to release the intermediate values. On the other hand, if a synthetic dataset is first published with strong privacy, but other parties find the synthetic data to be too inaccurate for their purposes, it is possible to make another release with weaker privacy. In this process, the intermediate privacy bounds are naturally released.

> The exploration of the composition theorem is partial. There is no composition theorem for pure ex‑post privacy analogous to Theorems 4.4–4.6.

> Can you prove adaptive composition for pure and approximate ex‑post DP, or provide counterexamples/conditions?

Combining Theorem 3.3 of Rogers et al. (2016) with our Theorem A.1 gives an analogue of our Theorem 4.5 for pure and probabilistic ex-post privacy. We have added a note of this after Theorem A.1. We are not aware of an analogue to this theorem for approximate ex-post privacy, or analogues of Theorems 4.4 and 4.6 with any non-RDP ex-post privacy definition. Proving or disproving these theorems is likely non-trivial, especially for approximate ex-post privacy, as it is not clear how to account for composition with the other ex-post definitions. The fact that accounting for composition is easier in ex-post RDP is one of our main motivations for working with it. As our paper focuses on ex-post RDP, we leave studying the other cases to future work.

comment.value:
Thank you for the reviews. We have responded to each individually, and updated the submission with many of the suggested changes. Changes are highlighted in blue in the revised paper. The most important changes are: 
- We have added a comparison between our ex-post RDP-based bounds for the Brownian mechanism and the original bounds from Whitehouse et al. (2022) to Section 5.
- We have added discussion on how the privacy bounds in our experiment change when $\alpha$ is changed to Appendix D. This includes an ex-post variant of zero-concentrated DP (zCDP) that our mechanisms satisfy.
- We have added discussion on how ex-post privacy bounds should be interpreted, and on the limitations of ex-post RDP, to Section 7.

Since the first submission, we realised that it would be possible to implement an ex-post version of DP-SGD using Theorem 4.5, or Theorem 4.6 if checking accuracy on private validation data, contrary to what our previous discussion in Section 7 suggested. We are planning to include an additional experiment demonstrating this during the rebuttal.

comment.value:
We have finished the experiment we promised in the previous message, and have updated the submission with the results, in Appendix E. Changes since the previous update are highlighted in orange.

To summarise the experiment, we use Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 to implement a variant of DP-SGD, specifically DP-Adam. We apply it to fine-tune the last layer of a vision transformer model for image classification on CIFAR-10. See the updated submission (Appendix E) for a detailed description. We hope that this experiment provides further evidence of the practical significance of our theory.

comment.value:
This comment summarises the most significant updates to the paper. All of these are in the updated submission, highlighted either blue or orange.

**DP-SGD Experiment** We have added another experiment that implements a variant of DP-SGD with an ex-post privacy guarantee. The results show that our implementation is able to reach a minimum accuracy threshold while minimising an approximate ex-post privacy bound. We believe this experiment provides additional evidence that our work has potential to move both practice and theory, addressing a criticism of Reviewer 3cjJ.

**Brownian Mechanism Comparison** We have added a comparison on the Brownian mechanism to Section 5 (Figure 1), which shows that the bounds from Whitehouse et al. (2022) are at best equivalent to our ex-post RDP bound when converted to ex-post ADP. Note that this conversion has been proven only for ex-post RDP, but we conjecture that it holds for probabilistic ex-post privacy in the same way it does in the ex-ante setting. This addresses a question from Reviewer coYK.

**Dependence on $\\alpha$** We have added equations describing how the ex-post RDP bounds in the synthetic data experiment change when $\alpha$ changes, and an ex-post version of zero-concentrated DP (zCDP), to Appendix D. The ex-post zCDP definition is modeled after the relationship between ex-ante RDP and zCDP. The mechanisms in the experiment satisfy this definition by their relationships between $\alpha$ and $\epsilon$. This addresses a question from Reviewer f84H.

**Additional Discussion** We have added discussion on the limitations of ex-post RDP, and how ex-post privacy bounds should be interpreted, to Section 7. These address questions from Reviewer coYK.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission4406 by Area Chair L3E6

summary.value:
This paper studies post-processing immunity (PPI) in the accuracy-first ex-post differential privacy setting, noting that previous works on ex-post and Renyi DP that first prioritize accuracy and subsequently measure privacy cannot necessarily handle post-processing. This paper proposes a simple fix: include the realized privacy loss as part of the algorithm’s output so it is preserved through post-processing. Under this notion, the paper proves that pure ex-post DP and Renyi DP satisfy PPI (while probabilistic ex-post DP does not), establish adaptive composition for ex-post RDP, and re-analyze the Brownian mechanism in this framework.

Reviewers agreed that the idea is conceptually clear and technically sound, addressing a real gap in how ex-post privacy is formalized,  but viewed the contribution as largely definitional rather than substantive. The work formalizes PPI neatly but reviewers expressed concerns about the lack of new mechanisms, limited experimental evaluations, and otherwise evidence for its “accuracy-first” claims. Several reviewers also questioned the practical relevance of outputting and comparing per-run privacy guarantees. Overall, the paper offers a clean theoretical clarification of PPI in ex-post DP, though its impact would grow with broader composition results and a clearer practical narrative.

reviewer_concerns.value: As multiple reviewer questions were somewhat minor, I believe they should have been addressed by the rebuttal. However, I think two substantive concerns by Reviewer 3cjJ remain outstanding. In particular, concerns about the technical novelties and the practical novelties may still persist.

reviewer_scores.value: Given the above points, it is not immediately clear to me that any reviewer would have changed their score if they had been able to fully participate in the discussion phase.
